lessons.title: Master the Perfect ChatGPT Prompt Formula
objectives: Reuse one prompt skeleton instead of inventing the structure each time
Constrain an answer with explicit limits rather than hoping for the right length
Build a small personal library of prompts that already work
lessons.notes:
Module 3 taught you WHY a good prompt works. This lesson is about making that repeatable so you are not rebuilding it from nothing every morning.

A skeleton you can fill in for almost anything:

"You are [ROLE]. I need [TASK]. Context: [WHO I AM, WHO IT IS FOR, WHAT HAS ALREADY HAPPENED]. Constraints: [LENGTH, TONE, FORMAT, WHAT TO AVOID]. Here is an example of what good looks like: [PASTE]."

The part most people still leave out is CONSTRAINTS, and it is the part that decides whether the output is usable. "Under 100 words. No bullet points. No exclamation marks. Do not invent statistics. Kenyan English, not American." Every one of those is a correction you would otherwise make by hand afterwards, so putting it in the prompt is pure saved time.

Negative constraints deserve their own mention because they are so rarely used. If AI output keeps sounding like AI output, the fix is usually to name the specific habits you dislike and ban them: "do not open with 'In today's fast-paced world', do not use the word 'delve', do not end with a summary paragraph."

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — keep a PROMPT FILE. A plain note on your phone with the eight or ten prompts you actually reuse, each one already improved by the corrections you made last time. This is a smaller idea than a custom assistant and it costs nothing, and for most people it is the single habit that turns AI from an occasional novelty into part of the working day. Every time you correct an output by hand, ask whether that correction belongs in the saved prompt instead.
lessons.practice: Write the skeleton out once for a task you do weekly, filling in every slot including at least three negative constraints drawn from things you have actually had to fix before. Run it. Then start the prompt file: save that prompt, and add to it every time you improve one. Aim for five entries by the end of the week.

quiz.question: Which part of a prompt most often decides whether the output is usable as-is?
options: The constraints — length, tone, format, and what to avoid
The politeness of the request
The total length of the prompt
Whether you thanked the model

quiz.question: What should you do with a correction you make to AI output by hand?
options: Move it into the saved prompt so it is not needed next time
Nothing — corrections are part of the process
Report it to the provider
Switch tools

lessons.title: You're Using ChatGPT Wrong
objectives: Stop treating an AI assistant as a search engine that answers in paragraphs
Give the model your own material instead of asking it to supply the material
Name the tasks in your own week where AI is the wrong tool
lessons.notes:
The common mistakes are not about prompting technique. They are about what people think the tool is for.

MISTAKE ONE — using it as a search engine. Asking "what is the current price of X" of a model that is answering from training is the single fastest route to a confident wrong answer. If the question is factual and current, use a tool that searches and then open the source.

MISTAKE TWO — asking it to supply the substance. "Write a report on our Q3 sales" with no sales figures produces plausible fiction. The strongest use of these tools is almost always TRANSFORMATION: you bring the raw material — your notes, your numbers, your messy draft, your call transcript — and the AI restructures, tightens, summarises or explains it. Your material plus its shaping beats its material every time.

MISTAKE THREE — accepting the first answer. The first answer is a starting position, not a delivery.

MISTAKE FOUR — using it where it does not belong. It cannot tell you what your customers want; ask them. It cannot make a judgement call that is yours to make. It should not be the last reader of anything that goes out with your name on it.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — a fifth one that matters more here than in the videos: treating AI output as finished work you can sell. Clients paying for writing, design or research are paying for judgement. Using AI to get there faster is completely legitimate and everybody does it. Sending raw, unread AI output to a client is how freelancers lose accounts, and it is easy to spot. The value you add is the reading, the cutting, the checking and the local knowledge the model does not have.
lessons.practice: Write down the five things you have used AI for in the last week. Mark each one: was it TRANSFORMATION (you supplied the material) or GENERATION (it supplied the material)? For each generation task, ask whether you could have supplied real material instead — and if so, redo one of them that way and compare the two outputs.

quiz.question: What is the strongest general use of an AI assistant?
options: Transforming material you supply — restructuring, tightening, summarising, explaining
Generating facts and figures you do not have
Replacing search engines
Making business decisions on your behalf

quiz.question: Why is sending raw AI output to a client risky?
options: Clients pay for judgement, and unread output is both visible and unverified
AI output is illegal to sell
Clients can detect which model was used
AI output is always poorly written

lessons.title: How to Use ChatGPT for Content Creation (Custom Workflow)
objectives: Run content production as a repeatable workflow rather than ad-hoc prompting
Feed the model your own voice so the output does not sound generic
Turn one piece of content into several formats without rewriting it each time
lessons.notes:
This lesson puts chaining and saved prompts together into something you can run every week.

A workflow that holds up:

1. IDEAS — from a real source, not from the model's imagination. Your customer questions, your comments, your competitors' posts, what people actually ask you. Paste those in and ask it to group them into themes.

2. ANGLE — pick one theme and have it propose several angles. You choose. This is a judgement step and it stays yours.

3. OUTLINE — structure before prose, always. Fix the structure here, where fixing is cheap.

4. DRAFT — section by section, in your voice. Which brings us to the part that matters most.

VOICE. The reason AI content sounds like AI content is that nobody gives it anything to imitate. Paste three things you have written that sound like you and say "match this voice — sentence length, vocabulary, how formal, how I open and close." This one step does more for quality than every other technique on this page combined.

5. REPURPOSE — one good piece becomes a LinkedIn post, a WhatsApp broadcast, a short video script, a newsletter. "Turn this into X, keeping the same voice." This is where the time saving actually lives, not in the drafting.

6. EDIT — you, reading it properly. Cut the padding, check every claim, add the one specific local detail the model could never know. That detail is what makes it yours.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the bottleneck for most people was never writing speed, it was showing up consistently. A workflow you run every Monday beats a brilliant prompt you use twice.
lessons.practice: Run the full six steps once, end to end, on a real piece of content you actually intend to publish. Time it. At step four, paste in three samples of your own writing and instruct it to match your voice — then compare that draft against the same draft without the samples. Publish the result and keep the workflow as a saved prompt.

quiz.question: What is the most effective way to stop AI content sounding generic?
options: Paste in several samples of your own writing and instruct it to match that voice
Ask it to 'be creative and original'
Use a longer prompt
Generate more drafts and pick the best

quiz.question: Where does most of the real time saving in a content workflow come from?
options: Repurposing one finished piece into several formats
Writing the first draft faster
Generating more ideas
Skipping the editing step

lessons.title: How to Use ChatGPT's Deep Research to Save Hours on Research
objectives: Commission a long research task with a brief rather than a question
Read a research report critically, starting from its sources
Know which research questions these tools handle badly
lessons.notes:
Deep research modes work differently from ordinary chat: the tool goes away for several minutes, reads many pages, and returns a structured report with citations. Several assistants now offer a version of this. The technique is the same in all of them, so learn the technique.

You are not asking a question, you are WRITING A BRIEF. A weak request is "research the poultry market in Kenya." A real brief says:

- The DECISION it feeds. "I am deciding whether to start with layers or broilers in Kiambu."
- The SCOPE. Kenya, last two years, small-scale operations.
- The QUESTIONS, listed. Feed costs, time to first income, common failure points, where people sell.
- The FORM you want it back in. Sections, a comparison table, sources against each claim.
- What to EXCLUDE. No large-scale commercial operations, no non-African markets.

Then — and this is the part people skip because the report looks so authoritative — READ IT SCEPTICALLY, from the sources up. Check where each significant number came from. A well-formatted report with confident figures and thin sources is worse than no report, because it makes you feel informed.

What these tools are genuinely good at: surveying an unfamiliar area quickly, finding what the main considerations are, and telling you what you do not yet know.

What they are bad at, and this matters here: anything that lives OFFLINE or in local knowledge. Real prices at your local market, what a council actually requires this month, which suppliers are reliable in your town, what your competitor down the road charges. Very little of that is on the indexable web. Use the report to arrive at the right questions, then get those answers by phone and on foot.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — these runs are slow and heavy. Write the brief carefully once rather than firing three lazy ones.
lessons.practice: Write a full brief — decision, scope, listed questions, output form, exclusions — for something you genuinely need to know, and run it. Then audit the report: pick the three most important claims in it and trace each one to its source. Write down which of the three actually held up, and list the questions you now need to answer locally, by phone or in person.

quiz.question: What should you give a deep research tool instead of a question?
options: A brief: the decision it feeds, the scope, listed questions, the output form, and exclusions
A single broad topic so it can explore freely
A list of websites to read
The answer you expect, to confirm

quiz.question: Which research question will such a tool handle worst?
options: Current real prices and requirements in your own town
An overview of an unfamiliar industry
The main considerations in a decision
What the common failure points of a business model are

lessons.title: 7 AI Freelance Services You Can Offer as a Beginner
objectives: Describe an AI service by the outcome it delivers, not the tool it uses
Pick a first service that matches what you can already show
Price the result rather than the hour
lessons.notes:
Nobody buys 'AI services'. They buy more listings written, a tidier inbox, a report they do not have to read, a month of posts they did not have to think about. Lead with the outcome; the tool is your business, not theirs.

Services that a beginner can genuinely sell:

PRODUCT DESCRIPTIONS AND LISTINGS — for shops selling online. Volume work, easy to demonstrate, easy to price per item.

SOCIAL CONTENT PACKS — a month of posts with captions and images, in the client's voice. Sell the month, not the post.

SUMMARISING — long documents, reports, meeting recordings turned into one page that a busy person will actually read.

BASIC WEB AND BIO COPY — small businesses with no website copy at all, which is most of them.

DATA TIDYING — messy spreadsheets and pasted lists cleaned, categorised and standardised.

CV AND PROFILE REWRITES — individuals, fast turnaround, and the course catalogue already has a course on doing this properly.

SETTING UP A CUSTOM ASSISTANT — from Module 5. Build a business its own assistant, loaded with its price list and tone. This is the most defensible of the seven because it leaves the client with an asset and it is hard for them to copy from a tutorial.

PRICING. Charge for the outcome. If a client learns you produced thirty listings in forty minutes, an hourly rate punishes you for being good at this. Per item, per pack, per month.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — your first sale will almost certainly not come from a global freelance platform, where you are competing on price with everyone on earth. It comes from a business you can walk into. Pick one, do the work unasked, show them the result, and name a price. Three such visits beats three hundred online proposals.
lessons.practice: Choose ONE service from the list. Do it for free, unasked, for a real local business — write the listings, build the content pack, clean the spreadsheet — and take it to them finished. Ask for nothing the first time except whether it is useful and what they would change. Then name a price for doing it monthly. That completed sample is now your portfolio.

quiz.question: How should an AI service be described to a client?
options: By the outcome delivered — more listings, a tidier inbox, a month of posts
By which AI model you use
By how many prompts it takes
By how fast AI is improving

quiz.question: Why is hourly pricing a poor fit for AI-assisted work?
options: It penalises you for delivering the same result faster
Clients never pay hourly rates
It is not allowed on freelance platforms
AI work cannot be timed

lessons.title: How Productizing AI Services Can 10X Your Revenue
objectives: Turn a custom service into a fixed package with a fixed scope and price
Recognise which part of your delivery is repeatable and which is judgement
Move a client from one-off work onto a monthly arrangement
lessons.notes:
Productising means selling the same defined thing repeatedly instead of quoting fresh for every job. Ignore the '10X' in the title — that is a headline, not a forecast. The real mechanism is duller and more reliable: you stop paying the cost of scoping, quoting and inventing a process every single time.

What a package needs to state, in writing, before you sell it:

WHAT THEY GET — exact and countable. "Twenty product listings, each under 60 words, with a title and three bullet points."
WHAT IT COSTS — one number.
HOW LONG IT TAKES — a stated turnaround you can actually hit.
HOW MANY REVISIONS — two, say. This single line is what stops a fixed price turning into unlimited work, and leaving it out is the mistake that ruins fixed-price work for beginners.
WHAT IS NOT INCLUDED — photography, publishing to their site, product strategy.

Then build the delivery once: the saved prompts, the custom assistant, the checklist, the template you send at the end. Each repeat gets faster while the price stays the same, and that — not AI speed alone — is where the margin is.

Be clear-eyed about what does NOT compress. Understanding an unfamiliar business, checking facts, handling a client who does not know what they want, and taking responsibility for what goes out: these stay human and they stay slow. Packages that pretend otherwise fall apart on the third client.

THE RETAINER. One-off work means hunting every month. The same package sold monthly — "twenty listings a month, KSh X" — is the difference between freelancing and having a business. Ask for it after you have delivered well twice, not before.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — write your package on one page and show it to someone who is not in this field. If they cannot tell you exactly what they would receive and what it costs, it is not a package yet.
lessons.practice: Write a one-page package for the service you delivered in the last lesson: deliverables stated in countable terms, price, turnaround, revision limit, and exclusions. Show it to one person outside your field and ask them to tell you back what they would get for the money. Rewrite until they get it right first time — then offer it to the business you already helped, as a monthly arrangement.

quiz.question: Which line most protects a fixed-price package from turning into unlimited work?
options: A stated limit on the number of revisions
A higher price
A longer turnaround time
A list of the AI tools used

quiz.question: Which part of delivering an AI service does NOT get faster with repetition?
options: Understanding an unfamiliar business and taking responsibility for the output
Producing the drafts
Formatting the deliverable
Sending the final package
